title: Srila Krishnadasa Babaji
html:
The Beloved Servant of Srila Bhaktivinoda

Among the disciples of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura there was one whom Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, after his departure, called “the beloved servant of Sri Bhaktivinoda Thakura,” “the best of devotees” and “the wanderer”: Srila Krishnadasa Babaji. His biographer calls him Srila Krishnadasa Babaji Maharaja, Babaji Mahashaya or simply Krishnadasa, and speaks of him as magnanimous (mahanubhava); another biography mentions him only briefly, as one more disciple of the Thakura. His father named him Indrachandra; the name Krishnadasa Babaji he received when the Thakura gave him the initiation of a paramahamsa.

His life was short, and almost all of it was spent in the service of his guru. We know of it from one biography, written soon after his departure, and above all from the memorial address Srila Bhaktisiddhanta gave at a gathering in his honor. The acharya's word is our principal primary source: where the biography differs from it, we follow the acharya; passages from it are given in our own translation from the Bengali.

Family and Youth

Indrachandra was born into a vaishya family in the village of Chhatra, in the Narail subdivision of the Jessore (Yashohar) district, on the 11th of Shravana, 1290 of the Bengali era, at eight in the morning — by our reckoning about 26 July 1883.1 The days of his appearance and departure are not in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

While his son was still a child, his father left household life to worship the Lord and accepted sannyasa in Hrishikesha. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls him Srila Narottama Dasa Yativara, “the best of renunciants”; the sources do not preserve his mother's name. Besides Indrachandra the family had two more brothers and two sisters; the sisters, the biography says, were still living when it was written.

The boy received his early schooling from his maternal uncle in the village of Binodpur. But when his father left home, Indrachandra, as the eldest, had to break off his schooling and come back to the family house. He supported the household on the income of his father's estate and of a small trade of his own, and paid for the schooling of the middle brother. As Krishna willed, that brother reached the final school class — and then passed away; soon the other brother too was gone.

The Search for a Guru

His father had left home, both brothers had left this life — and Indrachandra saw how barren and fleeting worldly life is. He was a thoughtful young man, and he began to seek a pure path to the highest goal. His sincere search brought him to the essential truth: Sriman Mahaprabhu alone bestows causeless mercy on the jivas, and under the shelter of that Magnanimous Lord one attains love for Krishna. Hearing the rudiments of Vaishnava practice current in his region, his mind rose higher, and he longed to take shelter at the feet of a mahanta-guru, a great teacher full of love for Hari and blessed by Mahaprabhu.

There were three such seekers: together with two friends Indrachandra twice came on foot to Navadvipa-dhama. In 1314 and early 1315 of the Bengali era (about 1907–1908) they were blessed with the darshan of the feet of a certain paramahamsa babaji, ever absorbed in extraordinary service to Sri Vishnu.2 Through his mercy and counsel the three “inquirers into the truth of Krishna” came to Srimad Bhaktivinoda Thakura.

The Thakura foresaw the good that awaited Indrachandra and gave him pancharatrika diksha. Then in Phalguna 1315 (about February–March 1909), seeing his worth, he also gave him the initiation of a paramahamsa (paramahamsya-samskara), so that nothing should hinder his worship of Krishna. From then on the Vaishnava world knew him as Srila Krishnadasa Babaji. Having accepted the dor-kaupina, the renunciant's cloth, he drove out of his heart both worldly people and worldly things entirely.

The Counted Name

The Thakura told him to sing the name of Krishna loudly day and night — and yet to keep count of the names (sankhya-nama). His guru's instruction took hold of his heart: one who chants in this way does not let inattention disturb his bhajana. Whoever heard the counted Name sung in his sweet voice understood that “Hare Krishna” from the lips of a sadhu differs from a worldly utterance of the name as a true thing differs from a fake.

In Sri Kshetra

At the beginning of 1316 (about the spring of 1909), at the wish of the Thakura, his “Acharya Prabhu,” Krishnadasa Babaji went to Sri Kshetra — Puri — and lived there for a year and a half. No contact with worldly people clouded his heart: the heartfelt mercy of his guru, the “Bhagavatacharya Prabhu,” kept him. Many who wore the renunciant's dress accepted invitations and gifts from worldly people; he accepted neither. He knew that even in alms gathered by the handful (madhukari) from a worldly man's hand lies the seed of worldliness, and he took nothing as alms from anyone who was not a Vaishnava. Nor did the usual errors of such “renunciants” touch him: taking dakshina at invitations — for which, his biographer says, they are liable to Yama's punishment — calling people together for crowded collective performances, and praising the begging of alms from householders who are strangers to the Vaishnavas.

There, in Purushottama, Sri Gaurahari once put him to the test. The Lord sent him a hypocrite in the guise of a renunciant, one of those who merely wear a devotee's dress. The man invited Krishnadasa into a society of pretended devotees, tempted him with a pilgrimage on foot to Vrindavana along the forest paths, and assured him that serving the sampradaya and guarding his guru's ashrama — these transcendental duties of bhakti — were actually to his own harm. But by the pure mercy of the same Gaurahari, Krishnadasa saw through the deceit. He understood that false renunciation (phalgu-vairagya) ruins the pure wealth of the Vaishnava sampradaya and is worthless; that pilgrimages on foot for one's own gain and other ritual deeds serve enjoyment and are opposed to “service of the guru with trust” (vishrambhena guroh seva), a limb of bhakti that Srila Rupa Gosvami names among the first (“Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu” 1.2.74); and that no service of worldly things can compare with service to Sri Gurudeva. So the foolish pretender's wiles did him no harm.

Far from his guru, he remained with him even in Kshetra: every day he served him by worshipping his image in a photograph (alokachitra-murti). For a disciple the guru's image is not a picture in the worldly sense: serving it, he served the Thakura himself, and this was one of his fixed duties in Puri.

Serving the Thakura

On his return from Kshetra, Krishnadasa Babaji served Thakura Bhaktivinoda with undivided devotion day and night — all sixty dandas of the day — until the Thakura's departure. One biography finds him beside the Thakura at Svananda-sukhada-kunja in Godruma as early as the spring of 1910, when Jagadisha Bhakti Pradipa received initiation there.3

One who accepts the tridanda gives body, mind and speech — his whole pure nature — to the service of Krishna and His devotees. Krishnadasa embraced that ideal wholly. He honored his “Acharya Prabhu” as the guru of all devotees (sarva-bhaktimatam guru) and revealed to all that service to such a guru is the source of devotion to Krishna, for the guru is the manifestation of the Lord's own mercy. That service, says his biographer, was the seed from which the creeper of his bhakti grew, and it has now brought him to eternal service in a kunja on the bank of Radha-kunda — to service at the feet of the Lord of Svananda-sukhada-kunja and of his own Mistress (nijadhishvari).4

The same service to his guru appeared in his heart as unfeigned love for all who had taken shelter of the Thakura, and as mercy that sought their true welfare. When the Thakura was leaving this world, everything that falls to the first disciple and the most beloved of those he had blessed was performed by none other than Srila Krishnadasa.

As the reward of his service to the Thakura while the Thakura was in this world, Krishnadasa's modest learning swelled into a river: he became an expert in the “Srimad-Bhagavata,” that ocean of bhakti-rasa. In him one saw the very life to which the “Bhagavata” leads; serving Hari according to the “Bhagavata,” he gained his place among the followers of Sri Rupa, the rupanugas.

Subtleties of Siddhanta, and Humility

By his guru's mercy he understood the subtle difference between separation (vipralambha) and union (sambhoga), and he grew anxious whenever he saw in a devotee the vice of the “doctrine of sambhoga” (sambhoga-vada). He knew clearly what is opposed to bhakti: the thirst for enjoyment of the karmis, who seek rasa for the sake of enjoyment; the thirst for renunciation of the jnanis; the talk of those seeking liberation that the fruit of the Name is control of mind and senses (shama and dama); and the pride of being a guru and the preaching of bhakti for the sake of prestige in a pretended devotee. He knew too that to attain rasa or prema suddenly, bypassing the gradual path (krama-pantha), is impossible, and that to acquire learning, wealth and honor in this world for one's own pleasure or for one's bodily kin, and to spend them on those people, is to diminish bhakti.

He knew the countless subtleties of siddhanta by heart, but did not disclose them unless he saw one fit to receive them. Never did he speak a word that wounded anyone's heart. He himself gave pancharatrika diksha to no one and did not even regard himself as anyone's shiksha-guru. And yet, seeing the countless people blessed by Sri Thakura Narottama, Sri Thakura Bhaktivinoda and other divine sages (divya-suri), he never presumed to judge that the company of those great souls did people no good: he understood that to bestow mercy on many was their calling. So in him strictness towards himself was joined with reverence for the acharyas.

Departure

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta begins his memorial address thus:

“Srila Krishnadasa Babaji, the beloved servant of Sri Bhaktivinoda Thakura, left the earthly world on the 10th of Ashvina, 1915 by the English reckoning, on the krishna-chaturthi, at two in the afternoon, setting out on the great journey (mahaprasthana) to the lotus feet of his Prabhupada [Srila Bhaktivinoda]” (our translation).

By our reckoning this was 27 September 1915 (1322 of the Bengali era).5 He departed in his native village, before his father and mother, “leaving with them the body they had given,” having completed, in the acharya's words, twenty-eight years and two months. “On the day Babaji Mahashaya turned twenty-seven,” says Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, “his master disappeared from him; exactly a year and two months later the devotee went to his master” (our translation).6

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta last saw him on the 20th of Bhadra (about 5–6 September 1915). Krishnadasa told him of his bodily
illness. “Unable to bear the account of the suffering of one as dear
to us as he was, we went elsewhere,” the acharya recalls (our
translation). These are words not of indifference but of love: the pain of one so dear to him in spirit was more than
he could bear.

Before leaving his body, Krishnadasa Babaji asked that what remained of his body be taken to Sri Dhama, and that money from worldly people never, under any circumstances, be accepted for anything connected with him. So to the very end he kept what he had been faithful to all his life: service accepts no gifts from those who live for worldly ends. Following the rules for paramahamsas, the samadhi rite was held at Svananda-sukhada-kunja in Godruma, on the day of Ekadashi — by our reckoning about 4 October 1915 — beside the samadhi of Sri Thakura.

The Acharya's Word

The grief of those faithful to the Thakura, writes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, cannot be put into words. All who beheld the beauty of his supremely pure life of service to the guru found a new joy; the pure devotees, bereft of the Thakura, took some comfort in seeing his serene and gentle form. What pain the departure of this wanderer caused their hearts, Sri Gaurahari alone knows. And where he has gone is the innermost chamber of Goloka, which the followers of Sri Rupa serve.

“By glorifying Srila Krishnadasa we are blessed; his company blessed our life,” says the acharya, and he closes by addressing him directly: Krishnadasa is in the eternal abode and has attained the service of Krishna, while “we,” bereft of his company, remain in the world and busy with worldly things; his heartfelt love was a step on “our” path of bhakti while he was here — may his eternal, causeless mercy rest now as well on those who, like “us,” have turned away from Hari. So humbly does the acharya speak of himself. Blessed are his father and mother, the parents of a pure Vaishnava: their household life surpasses the renunciation of those who have turned away from Hari. For what decides everything is not one's station in life but one's turning towards Hari; and his father was himself a renunciant. The place of his birth and the place where he left this world are glorified by him.

Notes

  1. The year of birth given in the biography does not agree with Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's memorial address. From 1883 to the autumn of 1915 is thirty-two years, whereas the acharya says that Krishnadasa departed having completed twenty-eight years and two months, and that he turned twenty-seven on the day of Srila Bhaktivinoda's departure (23 June 1914). That points rather to 1887 (1294 of the Bengali era); nor does the month of birth (Shravana) agree with the day of the Thakura's departure. Perhaps the years are counted differently here, or the year in the biography is in error; we give the biography's date without correcting it.
  2. The biography does not name this paramahamsa. Place, time and title naturally bring to mind Srila Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji Maharaja, but the sources do not say so, and we cannot assert it.
  3. According to the biography we chiefly follow, Krishnadasa Babaji went to Puri at the beginning of 1316 of the Bengali era (about the spring of 1909) and stayed there a year and a half, that is, until about the autumn of 1910. The accounts disagree — or the biography that places him in Godruma in the spring of 1910 is imprecise about the time.
  4. What is meant is the eternal, spiritual kunja at Radha-kunda after which the Thakura's bhajana-kutir in Godruma is named; we give the biographer's words as they stand, without elaborating on them.
  5. By our reckoning the 10th of Ashvina and the krishna-chaturthi of Ashvina 1322 of the Bengali era fall on the same day (±1 day). This day is not in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. The departure day of “Sripada Krishnadasa Babaji Maharaja” recorded there in spring, on the krishna-panchami of the month of Madhusudana, is evidently that of his namesake Akinchana Krishnadasa Babaji, a disciple of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, and not of the subject of this article.
  6. Srila Bhaktivinoda departed on 23 June 1914; by our count a year and three months passed until 27 September 1915. We give the acharya's words as they stand.
